content: Eclampsia, characterized by the occurrence of seizures in the context of pre-eclampsia, is a rare but potentially fatal condition. Magnesium sulphate is considered the first-line treatment for managing eclampsia. This review evaluates the effectiveness of magnesium sulphate and other anticonvulsants in preventing eclampsia. A total of 15 randomized trials were included in this review. Six of these trials, involving 11,444 women, compared magnesium sulphate with either a placebo or no anticonvulsant treatment. Magnesium sulphate was found to reduce the risk of eclampsia by more than half (risk ratio [RR] 0.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.29 to 0.58). The number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) was 100 (95% CI 50 to 100). Although there was a non-significant reduction in maternal death (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.10), there was no clear difference in serious maternal morbidity (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.32). Magnesium sulphate also reduced the risk of placental abruption (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.83; NNTB 100, 95% CI 50 to 1000). However, it was associated with a slight increase in the rate of caesarean sections (RR 1.05, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.10). There was no significant difference in the rates of stillbirth or neonatal death (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.15). Side effects were more frequently reported with magnesium sulphate, with 24% of women experiencing adverse effects, primarily flushing, compared to 5% in the control group (RR 5.26, 95% CI 4.59 to 6.03). The number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) was 6 (95% CI 5 to 6). One trial provided follow-up data comparing magnesium sulphate with placebo. Among 3,375 women, there was no significant difference in mortality (RR 1.79, 95% CI 0.71 to 4.53) or morbidity potentially related to pre-eclampsia (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.26) at a median follow-up of 26 months. For 3,283 children exposed to magnesium sulphate in utero, there was no significant difference in mortality (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.84) or neurosensory disability (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.58) at 18 months of age. When compared to other anticonvulsants, magnesium sulphate was more effective in reducing the risk of eclampsia. It was superior to phenytoin (three trials, 2,291 women; RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.60) and nimodipine (one trial, 1,650 women; RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.77). In conclusion, magnesium sulphate reduces the risk of eclampsia by more than half and may also lower the risk of maternal death. However, it does not appear to have a significant impact on long-term outcomes after hospital discharge. Approximately one-quarter of women treated with magnesium sulphate report side effects, most commonly flushing.
